Attested Tool-Server Admission:
A Security Extension to the
Model Context Protocol

Alfredo Metere Affiliation: Enclawed LLC Email: alfredo.metere@enclawed.com
August 24, 2026
Preprint: arXiv:2605.24248 ⋅\,\cdot\, Archived record: doi:10.5281/zenodo.20349263
Abstract

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how a large-language-model (LLM) agent and an external tool server exchange messages, but not trust: a host reads a server’s self-declared tool list and dispatches calls, with no notion of which servers it may use, at what sensitivity, or which of a server’s tools are in bounds. This work grew out of a concrete need — letting the Enclawed agent use Google’s externally-operated MCP servers (Gmail, Calendar, Drive) safely, admitting the server and bounding the tools it may drive, without changing MCP or Enclawed’s own tool application-programming interface (API). The mechanism we built, mcp-attested (shipped in both the open enclawed-oss distribution and the enclaved flavor), generalizes: the gap that makes an unmediated third-party connection unsafe for one user makes a regulated deployment impossible to accredit. We close it with three additive mechanisms: (1) a small, offline-signed clearance assertion a server publishes at a well-known Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) and a host verifies against a pinned trust root before any tool dispatch; (2) a deny-by-default per-server tool allowlist, so admitting a server is not trusting its every tool; and (3) a flavor-gated enforcement mode that turns the checks from warnings into hard denials, with every decision written to a tamper-evident audit log. We give the wire format, the verification algorithm, a security analysis, and an LLM-driven adversarial evaluation; we then state the design in normative Request-for-Comments (RFC 2119) form — schema, verification rules, error registry, well-known registration, and machine-checkable conformance vectors — so it can be adopted as an MCP addendum rather than reinvented. An unextended host ignores the well-known document and behaves exactly as today.

1 Introduction

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) [2, 1] standardized something the agent ecosystem badly needed: a single way for an LLM-driven host to enumerate the tools, resources, and prompts that an external server offers, and to invoke them over a uniform JSON-RPC (JavaScript Object Notation remote procedure call) [10] envelope. Its adoption was rapid precisely because it is minimal. A host connects to a server over a transport (a subprocess pipe, stdio; the HyperText Transfer Protocol, HTTP; or a streaming variant), issues tools/list, receives a list of tool descriptors, and thereafter issues tools/call with a tool name and an arguments object.

Where this work began.

We wanted the Enclawed agent to use Google’s externally-operated Workspace MCP servers (Gmail, Calendar, Drive) as ordinary tools. Wiring them in the obvious way trusts whatever tool list the server advertises and hands the model the server’s entire surface — including, say, a “delete every message” tool — the moment it connects. We wanted instead to admit such a server deliberately and bound the tools the agent can drive, without changing MCP or Enclawed’s own tool API. The component built for that, mcp-attested, generalizes into the extension this paper proposes; it ships in both the open enclawed-oss distribution and the enclaved flavor.

That minimalism is the security gap. MCP is silent on whether a host should talk to a given server, what sensitivity may cross the connection, and which subset of the server’s advertised tools the host may drive; the tool list and the server’s identity — beyond whatever its Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificate asserts — are taken on faith. The result is a confused deputy [7]: an LLM steered by adversarial context [18, 13] calls a tool, and nothing sits between that decision and the network write.

An unmediated connection is unsafe in every deployment: the operator chose the server, but not the tool surface the model can reach, and a prompt-injected model can drive a destructive tool — deleting a mailbox, say — on a server the operator never authorized at that granularity [5]. A lone operator on their own laptop may absorb that risk; a bank, a hospital, or a government program putting an agent on regulated data cannot — and, with no admission record, cannot even prove what happened. A control framework such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publication (SP) 800-53 [15] expects least-privilege access enforcement (AC-3, AC-6), information-flow enforcement between sensitivity levels (AC-4), and an audit record of access decisions (AU-2, AU-9). None of these can be satisfied if the host has no notion of which server is which, at what level, or which tools are in bounds.

Contribution.

This paper documents mcp-attested, the MCP admission layer, and generalizes it into a standards-style proposal. The design rests on a single observation: MCP needs a trust layer, but that layer can be added entirely above the existing protocol — one server-published document and one host-side gate — without changing a single existing MCP message (Figure 1). Concretely we contribute:

  1. 1.

    A clearance assertion format (Section 4): a tiny, offline-signed JSON document, published by a server at the well-known URI /.well-known/enclawed-clearance.json, that binds the server’s identity to a sensitivity clearance and is verifiable against a host-local trust root. We reuse the exact byte-canonicalization and Ed25519 [9] signing flow already used for signing Enclawed extension manifests, so a server operator signs a clearance assertion with the same offline tool they already use for code.

  2. 2.

    An admission algorithm (Section 5): the host verifies signature, signer authority, and clearance ordering before the first tool dispatch, and treats admitting a server as distinct from authorizing its tools by binding each admitted server to a closed, per-server tool allowlist (Section 5.3).

  3. 3.

    A flavor-gated enforcement model (Section 5.2): in the open flavor the checks are advisory (warn-but-allow, preserving drop-in compatibility); in the enclaved flavor they are hard denials. Every decision — allow, deny, or warn — is appended to a hash-chained audit log.

  4. 4.

    An adversarial evaluation (Section 7): we turn each stated property into an executable test driven by an LLM-generated red-team corpus (tool-name evasions and forged clearance assertions) and report the results — every evasion denied with zero leaked network writes and every forgery denied at the expected guard, across both a hand-written suite and a large model-generated coverage campaign.

  5. 5.

    A security analysis and a standardization argument (Sections 6 and 8): we state the properties the extension provides, the residuals it does not, its FIPS-mode compatibility, and why it is small and generic enough to be an MCP extension rather than a fork.

We are explicit about scope. This is an admission and information-flow extension. It does not by itself stop a malicious admitted server from misbehaving within its granted tools, nor does it police the content crossing an admitted connection; those are the jobs of, respectively, skill capability containment [12] and the egress reference monitor [11], which compose with this layer but are out of scope here. What this layer guarantees is that the host only ever speaks to servers whose identity and clearance it has cryptographically checked, only ever drives tools it has pre-authorized on those servers, and records every such decision.

Availability and status.

This is a report on a shipping system, not a proposal. Every mechanism described here — the clearance assertion and its verifier, the per-server tool allowlist, flavor-gated enforcement, and the hash-chained audit log — is implemented and runs in production in both the open enclawed-oss distribution and the accredited enclawed-enclaved build. The only parts not yet shipped are the items Section 11 explicitly marks as future work (per-tool clearance, per-assertion freshness/revocation, and submission of the normative extension).

2 Background: MCP and its security posture

2.1 What MCP specifies

MCP defines a client–server protocol carried over JSON-RPC 2.0. A host embeds one or more clients; each client maintains a session with a server that exposes some combination of tools (callable functions), resources (readable content), and prompts. After an initialize handshake that negotiates capabilities and protocol version, the standard interaction for tool use is:

  • •

    tools/list →\rightarrow an array of tool descriptors, each with a name, a human-readable description, and a JSON-Schema for its arguments;

  • •

    tools/call with { name, arguments } →\rightarrow a structured result.

The transport may be a local subprocess pipe (stdio) or a network channel (HTTP, optionally with server-sent-event streaming). When the channel is network-facing, confidentiality and server endpoint authentication are whatever the underlying TLS [20] provides; recent revisions of the spec layer OAuth [6] on top for user authorization to a server.

2.2 What MCP does not specify

The protocol’s trust assumptions, made explicit:

  1. 1.

    No host-side server admission. TLS authenticates that the host reached the endpoint named in the Uniform Resource Locator (URL); OAuth authorizes the user to the server. Neither answers the host’s question: “is this server one I am permitted to use as a tool provider, and at what sensitivity?” A valid certificate for evil.example is still a valid certificate.

  2. 2.

    No sensitivity / clearance notion. There is no field in which a server declares the data classification it is cleared to handle, and no host-side check that a server’s level dominates the level of the data the agent is about to send it. Information-flow control (Bell–LaPadula [3], AC-4) has no hook.

  3. 3.

    The tool list is self-asserted and trusted wholesale. The host learns the available tools from the server itself, and the typical host exposes all of them to the model. Admitting a server is implicitly admitting every tool it advertises, now and after any future tools/list change.

  4. 4.

    No standard audit of admission decisions. Because there is no admission step, there is nothing to record. AU-2/AU-9 evidence must be reconstructed from transport logs, if at all.

These gaps are not bugs in MCP; they are out of its chosen scope. The contribution of this paper is to fill them above the protocol, additively.

2.3 The Enclawed setting

Enclawed is a security-hardened distribution of an open agentic artificial-intelligence (AI) gateway, shipped in two flavors. The open flavor preserves drop-in compatibility with the upstream catalog and prefers warnings to denials. The enclaved flavor is deny-by-default and enforces Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) 140-3 [14] approved cryptography; it is the flavor an operator accredits against a control framework [5]. The same code path runs in both; a single runtime flavor value selects advisory versus enforcing behavior. mcp-attested is the component that brings MCP connections under this regime, in either flavor.

2.4 Running example: the Google Workspace bridge

We use one concrete deployment throughout — the one that motivated the work — and keep it faithful to the extension’s own executable test. The Enclawed agent is to use Google’s Gmail MCP server (endpoint gmailmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1) at the internal clearance level. Google operates the endpoint; Enclawed does not, and it publishes no Enclawed clearance assertion. The bundled, signed bridge extension mcp-google-workspace registers that endpoint with a closed tool allowlist of Gmail’s read/compose tools (e.g. list_labels, search_threads, create_draft). Three properties must hold simultaneously: (i) the connection is a deliberate, recorded admission, not an implicit consequence of the model dialing a URL; (ii) only the allowlisted tools are reachable — a prompt-injected request for a destructive tool such as delete_everything is refused before any network call, whatever the server’s tools/list advertises; and (iii) none of this changes Enclawed’s own tool API, so the user’s existing skills keep working. This is exactly the scenario the shipped admission test (client-admission.test.ts) exercises, and it passes against the shipping code. Section 5.2 gives the connection path for servers like Google that publish no clearance assertion of their own; Section 5.3 the tool gate; and Sections 4 and 5 the general case of a server that does publish one, of which the Google bridge is the no-server-side-assertion special case.

3 Threat model

Deployment.

We assume the Enclawed personal-assistant trust model: one operator (or one operating organization) per gateway instance; the host and its locally pinned trust root are part of the trusted computing base; the LLM is not. The agent’s instruction stream is assumed to be partially attacker-controlled through retrieved content, tool outputs, and message bodies — the standard prompt-injection posture [18, 13].

Adversary capabilities.

We consider an adversary who can:

  1. 1.

    inject instructions into the model’s context that steer it toward connecting to an attacker-chosen MCP server or invoking an attacker-chosen tool;

  2. 2.

    stand up a network MCP server with a valid TLS certificate for a domain they control;

  3. 3.

    present a self-declared tool list and a self-declared sensitivity level of their choosing;

  4. 4.

    replay or tamper with a legitimately-issued clearance assertion in transit (the host–server channel is assumed adversary-observable unless protected by TLS).

Adversary limits.

The adversary cannot forge an Ed25519 signature without a trust-root private key; cannot mutate the pinned trust root, which is locked after startup (Section 5.1); and is not, in the base model, a co-tenant on the host — the host and its pinned trust root are part of the trusted computing base. Multi-tenant adversarial isolation on one shared gateway is explicitly out of scope, consistent with the framework’s stated security model.

Goals.

Against this adversary the extension must guarantee: (G1) the host never enforces a connection as admitted to a server whose clearance assertion is missing, malformed, unsigned, signed by a key not in the trust root, signed by an expired key, signed by a key not authorized for the asserted level, whose asserted level is below what the call requires, or that is presented from a host outside the assertion’s signed origin list; (G2) the host never dispatches a tool the operator did not pre-authorize for that server, even if the server advertises it and the model requests it; (G3) every admission decision is recorded in tamper-evident storage; and (G4) the pinned trust root cannot be mutated at runtime to admit an otherwise-failing server.

Empirically demonstrated runtime exploits.

The trust gap above is not theoretical. Adversarial testing against unprotected multi-server MCP deployments has surfaced three exploitable runtime behaviors that bypass standard post-invocation defenses:

  1. 1.

    Tool-name shadowing. An untrusted or injected server registers a tool name that collides with a co-loaded legitimate tool surface, causing the host to route execution calls silently to the malicious server.

  2. 2.

    Dynamic schema drift. A malicious server advertises a benign schema during the initial tools/list handshake to pass static filters, then mutates parameter constraints or semantic requirements before the subsequent tools/call invocation.

  3. 3.

    Registry poisoning. Direct manipulation of the host’s tool cache via downstream prompt injection or unvetted secondary discovery layers.

Defender-side benchmarks across these vectors [8] show that relying on the model layer to detect them is a brittle, non-deterministic boundary: permissive personas completely fail to identify active schema drift, while catching tool-name shadowing imposes a reasoning load that degrades rapidly under context-window exhaustion. ATSA’s contribution is to move the security boundary from probabilistic, post-invocation reasoning to deterministic, cryptographic admission-time gating — preventing the prompt-injected model from ever accessing or driving an unvetted tool surface in the first place. Vectors 1 and 3 are closed at admission and tool-authorization time (Section 8.1); vector 2 — schema drift after a server is admitted — is structurally adjacent and is the subject of Section 9.

4 The clearance assertion

The first new artifact is a server-published clearance assertion: a small JSON document, served at the well-known URI [17] /.well-known/enclawed-clearance.json, that binds a server’s identity to a declared sensitivity level and is signed offline by a key the host trusts. Its shape is deliberately identical to the Enclawed extension manifest (enclawed.module.json), so a server operator signs it with the same offline procedure they already use to sign extension code, and the host verifies it with the same routines.

Fields.

clearance is a level in an ordered classification lattice (Section 4.1). capabilities must contain the literal "mcp-server"; this is what distinguishes a clearance assertion for an MCP endpoint from any other signed manifest using the same envelope. signerKeyId names a key the host expects to find in its trust root, and signature is an Ed25519 signature over the canonical serialization of every field except the signature itself. Two optional fields complete the envelope and also fall under the signature: netAllowedHosts binds the assertion to specific origins (enforced in Section 5), and verification records the producer’s verification level.

Definition 1 (Canonical body).

The canonical body of an assertion comprises exactly the fields v, id, publisher, version, clearance, capabilities, signerKeyId, verification, and netAllowedHosts; the signature field is excluded, and an absent signerKeyId is serialized as null. It is emitted as deterministic JSON in which every object’s keys are written in sorted (lexicographic) order and array members are sorted. Both signer and verifier compute exactly these bytes, so signing and verification cannot disagree on field order or whitespace.

Using one canonicalization for extension manifests and MCP clearance assertions is a deliberate attack-surface reduction: there is a single signing path, a single verification path, and a single place where a canonicalization bug could live, rather than one per document type.

4.1 The classification lattice

Clearance levels are not free-form strings; they are points in a totally ordered lattice with a numeric rank, so “does server level dominate required level” is a single integer comparison. The framework ships five built-in schemes — default, us-government, healthcare-hipaa, financial-services, and a generic-3-tier — and validates custom schemes loaded from JSON (ranks must be contiguous from 00). Three of the built-ins:

Rank default us-government healthcare-hipaa
0 PUBLIC UNCLASSIFIED PUBLIC
1 INTERNAL CUI INTERNAL
2 CONFIDENTIAL CONFIDENTIAL PHI
3 RESTRICTED SECRET SENSITIVE-PHI
4 RESTRICTED-PLUS TOP SECRET RESEARCH-EMBARGOED
5 SCI TS//SCI —

Each level carries aliases so an organization can speak its own dialect (SECRET for RESTRICTED, CUI for INTERNAL) while the engine compares ranks; the regulated schemes additionally define valid compartments (MENTAL-HEALTH, GENETICS, M_AND_A, …) and releasability markings (NOFORN, BAA-COVERED, …). This is what makes the same admission code sector-neutral: a financial-services deployment ranks MNPI above CONFIDENTIAL, a hospital ranks SENSITIVE-PHI above PHI, a government program uses the US-government ladder — the verifier is identical. (Markings above: CUI, Controlled Unclassified Information; SCI, Sensitive Compartmented Information; PHI, Protected Health Information; MNPI, Material Non-Public Information; NOFORN, Not Releasable to Foreign Nationals; BAA, Business Associate Agreement.)

Definition 2 (Domination).

Let rank⁡(ℓ)\mathrm{rank}(\ell) be the numeric rank of level ℓ\ell in the applicable ladder (level names are matched case-insensitively, canonical name or alias). A server at level ss meets a required level rr, written s⪰rs\succeq r, iff rank⁡(s)≥rank⁡(r)\mathrm{rank}(s)\geq\mathrm{rank}(r).

5 The admission algorithm

When the host is about to use an MCP server, it runs the verification below before treating the connection as admitted. The fetch step is injectable (so it can run over the mutually-authenticated TLS channel inside the enclave network, or be stubbed in tests); everything after it is pure and side-effect-free except for the audit append.

The order is security-relevant. Capability and signedness are cheap structural checks; signer lookup and the approvedClearance check establish authority (does the trust root let this signer vouch for this level?) before the cryptographic verification; the signature check establishes authenticity; and only then does the level comparison establish sufficiency. A server cannot self-promote: even a validly signed assertion is denied if the signing key is not authorized in the trust root for the level it claims.

5.1 The trust root

The trust root is a set of records, each pairing a keyId and an Ed25519 public key with an approvedClearance list — the maximum set of levels that key is allowed to vouch for. A development bundle ships three signers: a community signer and a bundled-extension signer, each approved only up to INTERNAL, and a high-tier reference signer approved up through RESTRICTED-PLUS for exactly the attested-MCP use case. Production deployments replace these with the operator’s own signers.

The crucial property is that the trust root is lockable. The enclaved bootstrap calls lockTrustRoot() immediately after seeding it; once locked, setTrustRoot() refuses further mutation. This binds the running binary to the deploying organization’s signers and removes “swap the trust root at runtime” from the adversary’s toolkit.

5.2 Connection gating and flavor semantics

The verifier returns a verdict; what the host does with a negative verdict depends on the flavor.

  • •

    Enclaved flavor: a negative verdict is a hard denial. The connection is not admitted, invoke returns an error, and an mcp.connect.deny record is appended to the audit log. This is the accreditable mode and satisfies goal G1.

  • •

    Open flavor: the same check runs, but a negative verdict is surfaced as a warning rather than masked. The client returns a non-OK result tagged “open flavor: warn-only” and writes an mcp.connect.warn record, leaving the host free to proceed if it explicitly chooses. Critically, the open path never silently rewrites a failure into a success — it refuses to return ok on a failed verification, so a warning can never be mistaken for a pass.

A successful verification in either flavor appends mcp.connect.allow with the resolved clearance and signer key id. There is also a deliberate first-party fast path: bundled bridges (e.g. a Google Workspace or GitHub bridge) whose own signed extension manifest and registry registration already constitute the admission decision may set skipClearancePreflight; this path still audits the allow, so no admitted connection is unrecorded. The fast path exists because public third-party MCP servers do not (yet) publish an Enclawed clearance assertion, and the bridge’s signed manifest is the equivalent gate (Section 8 returns to this).

5.3 Tool-level admission

Admitting a server is not authorizing its tools. This is the second new gate and the answer to gap 3 of Section 2.2. Each server the host will use is recorded in a registry entry binding the endpoint to: the owning bridge, the required clearance, a closed allowedTools list, and the transport. On every invoke:

Three things follow. First, the allowlist is a closed list: a tool the model requests that is not on it is denied and audited (mcp.tool.deny), regardless of what tools/list advertised — this is goal G2. Second, the clearance gate is re-run at dispatch, not just at first connect, so a connection cannot be admitted once and then reused indefinitely without re-checking. Third, an endpoint with no registry entry cannot be driven at all: there is no implicit “trust whatever the model dialed” path. The combination means a prompt-injected model that asks to call gmail.deleteAllMessages on a server whose allowlist contains only gmail.search is denied at the host, before any byte reaches the network.

5.4 Transport

Dispatch rides the existing MCP envelope unchanged: a JSON-RPC 2.0 tools/call over HTTP(S), with an optional Authorization: Bearer token supplied by a pluggable auth provider for servers that also do OAuth user-authorization. The extension adds no new message types to MCP; the clearance assertion is fetched out-of-band at a well-known URI, and the tool allowlist is enforced entirely host-side. An unextended MCP server is unaware that any of this happened.

5.5 Audit events

Every decision is an append to the framework’s hash-chained, optionally multi-witnessed audit log [5]. The event vocabulary is small and total over the decision space:

Event When Carries
mcp.connect.allow verification passed (or bridge fast-path) level, signerKeyId
mcp.connect.deny verification failed, enclaved flavor reason
mcp.connect.warn verification failed, open flavor reason
mcp.tool.deny tool not in server allowlist bridge, toolName

Because the log is hash-chained, the sequence of admission decisions is tamper-evident: an auditor can replay it and detect any excision or back-dating, which is what AU-9 asks for and what goal G3 requires.

6 Security analysis

We restate the guarantees as properties and argue each from the mechanism.

Property 1 (Authenticated, authorized admission).

In the enclaved flavor, a connection is enforced as admitted only if the server’s clearance assertion (a) declares the mcp-server capability, (b) is signed, (c) by a key present in the locked trust root, (d) whose notAfter (if set) has not passed, (e) that is approved for the asserted level, (f) the signature verifies over the canonical body, (g) the asserted level dominates the required level, and (h) when the assertion carries a signed host allow-list, the connected host is a member of it.

Argument. Each clause is a guarded DENY in Section 5 that precedes ALLOW; the conjunction is necessary. Forging (f) requires a trust-root private key (adversary limit); bypassing (c), (d), or (e) requires mutating the trust root, which is locked after startup (Section 5.1). A validly-signed assertion cannot have its level escalated, because the level is inside the signed body. Clause (h) closes cross-host replay: because netAllowedHosts is part of the signed canonical body, an attacker cannot retarget a valid assertion to a host the signer did not authorize without invalidating the signature; an assertion that omits the list remains origin-agnostic and relies, as before, on the enclave’s mutually-authenticated TLS and trust-root scoping. Our adversarial harness (Section 7) confirms clauses (a)–(h) fire as guarded denials, including a host-bound assertion replayed from a foreign origin and an assertion signed by an expired signer. ∎

Property 2 (Tool least-privilege).

An admitted server’s tool is dispatched only if it appears in that server’s closed allowedTools list, independent of what the server advertises or the model requests.

Argument. invoke checks isToolAdmitted against the registry entry before any transport call and denies otherwise; an unregistered endpoint has no dispatch path at all (Section 5.3). The server’s tools/list feeds the model’s options but not the host’s authorization. ∎

Property 3 (Decision auditability).

Every admission and tool-gating decision appends one event to a hash-chained log; the event set is total over {allow, deny, warn, tool-deny}.

Argument. Each return path in connect and invoke is preceded by an audit append (Section 5.5); the chain is tamper-evident by construction. ∎

Property 4 (Trust-root immutability).

Once locked at startup, the pinned trust root cannot be mutated, so the set of signers under which a server may be admitted cannot be widened at runtime.

Argument. lockTrustRoot() sets a one-way flag; thereafter setTrustRoot() raises TrustRootLockedError (Section 5.1). Integrity of the host binary itself is a trusted-computing-base assumption (Section 3), not a property this layer claims. ∎

Residuals (explicitly out of scope).

The extension does not provide: (i) protection against a correctly admitted, correctly cleared server that misbehaves within its allowed tools — that is the job of capability containment on the skill/tool side [12]; (ii) content inspection of data crossing an admitted connection — that is the egress reference monitor [11] and the data-loss-prevention (DLP) scanner, which run downstream; (iii) defense against an LLM that simply refuses to use a tool (a liveness, not safety, concern); (iv) multi-tenant adversarial isolation on one shared gateway, which the framework’s trust model excludes by design. These layers compose: a call must pass admission and clearance and tool-allowlist (this paper) and capability containment and egress screening before it leaves the host.

FIPS posture.

The admission path uses only Ed25519 (FIPS 186-5) and the Secure Hash Algorithm SHA-256 (FIPS 180-4), routed through the framework’s approved-algorithm enforcement, so it runs unmodified in a FIPS-mode enclaved deployment.

7 Evaluation

The properties of Section 6 are stated as arguments from the mechanism; this section turns each into an executable test and reports the result. The tests ship in the open enclawed-oss reference implementation (extensions/mcp-attested) and are reproducible with npx vitest run …/adversarial.test.ts.

7.1 Methodology

Hermetic, network-observing harness.

Every test runs against in-memory stubs, never a live server. Two seams make this faithful rather than merely convenient: the verifier’s fetcher argument supplies the clearance assertion, and the transport’s fetchImpl supplies tool-call responses. The transport stub increments a counter on every call, so a denial that nonetheless leaked a network write would be caught by an assertion that the counter is zero. A fake runtime installed through setRuntime() records every audit append, so the audit vocabulary of Section 5.5 is checked directly rather than inferred.

Faithful positives, single-mutation negatives.

Trust roots are seeded per test with freshly generated Ed25519 keypairs. Valid baselines are signed through exactly the production path (canonicalManifestBytes →\to signManifest); each negative is one targeted mutation of a baseline — drop the signature, swap the signer, upgrade the clearance field after signing, omit the mcp-server capability, and so on — so a test isolates exactly one guard of Property 1.

LLM-generated adversarial corpus.

The inputs are a red-team corpus authored by the LLM as if it were the attacker. For the tool-name gate it spans command-chaining (list_labels; delete_everything), case folding, whitespace and control-character injection, Unicode homoglyph / right-to-left-override (RTL) / zero-width tricks, path traversal, near-miss truncations, prototype-pollution probe strings (__proto__, constructor), and JSON smuggling. For the admission gate it spans unsigned, wrong-signer, signer self-promotion, signature tamper, post-signing body upgrade, capability omission, level shortfall, and malformed / transport error assertions.

7.2 Results

All 48 tests across the mcp-attested admission layer and its Google Workspace bridge pass (44 under vitest, 4 under node:test); the 20 adversarial tests are summarized below.

Property under test Inputs Outcome
Property 2 tool least-privilege 31 evasions all 31 denied (mcp.tool.deny); 0 network writes; only the 2 exact allowlisted names admitted
Property 1 authenticated, authorized admission 2 valid + 12 invalid both valid admitted (incl. a host-bound assertion from its own origin); all 12 denied, each at the expected guard (unsigned, not-in-root, expired-signer, not-approved, bad-signature, below-required, host-not-bound, …)
Auditability + flavor gating 3 paths enclaved fail →\to mcp.connect.deny; open fail →\to mcp.connect.warn and never ok; success →\to mcp.connect.allow

The harness is adversarial in substance.

Beyond confirming intended denials, the corpus surfaced a genuine origin-binding weakness in an earlier verifier — which is why the verifier now enforces the signed host allow-list (Property 1(h)). A from-scratch adversarial corpus that forces a real fix, rather than only re-confirming the happy path, is the evidence that the suite earns its name.

7.3 Dynamic and live conformance (gated)

Two further harnesses ship alongside the hermetic suite but depend on external prerequisites, so we describe their method rather than report numbers.

LLM-driven fuzzing.

A local model served by Ollama is asked, at run time, to red-team the gate — to emit tool-name evasions against a bridge allowlist and to forge clearance assertions that might slip past the verifier. Each generated tool name that is not an exact allowlist member must be denied with no network write, and each forged assertion must be rejected. Crucially, the security invariant is independent of the model’s quality: the model never holds a trust-root private key, so it cannot produce a verifying signature, and exact-match admission is immune to its surface tricks — a stronger model merely yields more inventive denials. The harness is enabled with OLLAMA_LIVE=1 and fails loudly if no model is reachable, so it never passes vacuously.

We ran a coverage campaign with llama3.2 served by Ollama 0.24.0 (Figure 2: 1500 generation rounds per phase at 6-way graphics-processing-unit (GPU) concurrency, deduplicated). Because the gate is deterministic — exact-match for tool names, an Ed25519 signature for assertions — a passing result is full coverage, not a deny probability: Table 1 reports how many distinct adversarial inputs the model produced and how many the gate denied. Of 27,025 unique tool-name evasions (from 47,945 generated) spanning whitespace/control, separator-chaining, near-miss, path-traversal, homoglyph/zero-width/RTL, and case-variant tricks, all were denied with zero network writes and none admitted. Of the model’s forged clearance assertions, 14,378 distinct ones survived JSON parsing and all were rejected (the model holds no trust-root private key, so a verifying signature is out of reach; malformed forgeries are discarded by the harness and would be denied in any case). This attacker-side campaign is complemented by independent defender-side baselines from the AlgoVoi Agent-Trust-Bench suite [8], whose differential profiles across 29-tool surfaces confirm that unprotected deployments remain uniformly vulnerable to the runtime routing and session exploits enumerated in Section 3.

Live end-to-end.

A second harness uses the local model as the agent brain driving the real Google Workspace bridge (Section 2.4) through the gate, with operator-supplied OAuth read only from the environment. It asserts the deterministic invariant — a tool outside the allowlist is denied before any network call — and, best-effort, that an allowlisted tool the model selects is dispatched to the live endpoint, with any failure on that path required to be a transport/scope error rather than an admission denial. It is gated behind GOOGLE_LIVE=1 plus operator credentials. We executed it against Google’s live Gmail MCP endpoint (gmailmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1, independently confirmed reachable with an HTTP 200 to tools/list) using an operator-supplied OAuth token: the gate admitted the allowlisted tool the model selected and dispatched it to the real endpoint with no admission denial, and denied the out-of-allowlist tool before any network call.

This keeps the headline numbers honest: the 48 hermetic tests reproduce anywhere with no setup, while the gated LLM-driven and live tests (the Ollama fuzz, the coverage campaign, and the live Gmail end-to-end) — which additionally require a local model and, for the Gmail path, operator credentials — were run and also pass. They are provided as operator-runnable conformance checks.

8 Why a protocol extension, and how to standardize it

The design choices above were made so that the mechanism is a candidate for a generic MCP extension, not just an Enclawed feature.

If it already works above MCP, why change the standard?

The natural objection: the extension is purely additive (below), so an integrator can bolt it on today without the maintainers lifting a finger — why ask them to do anything? Because additive is not interoperable. Bolted on by one vendor, attestation secures only that vendor’s island: a server’s signed clearance document means something only to hosts that already agreed, out of band, on its shape and verification order. The payoff — “this server is attested” as a claim any host can check, servers publishing one document instead of NN vendor dialects, and the protocol’s own SDKs shipping the gate on by default so security stops being each integrator’s opt-in — exists only once a single format is agreed. And only the specification owner can mint that agreement: no vendor can unilaterally make a well-known name and a verification order the ecosystem’s Schelling point, which is precisely why public MCP servers publish no attestation today (Section 5.2). The maintainers’ work is small, and is the part only they can do: reserve the well-known name and bless one document shape and verification order (Section 8.1) — the reference implementation and conformance vectors (Appendix D) already exist. That the mechanism rides entirely above MCP is what makes adoption cheap and low-risk, not a reason to defer it: it is an optional, additive addendum with no compatibility tax.

It is purely additive.

The clearance assertion lives at a well-known URI [17]; an unextended host never fetches it and is unaffected. The tool allowlist is host-side state; an unextended server never sees it. No existing MCP message changes shape. This is the same additive discipline that let OAuth, security.txt, and OpenID discovery ride the well-known mechanism without forking the protocols they extended.

It separates the three questions MCP conflates.

TLS answers “did I reach the named endpoint.” OAuth answers “is the user allowed to use this server.” The clearance assertion answers the missing third question: “is this server one my organization has authorized as a tool provider, and at what sensitivity.” These are orthogonal and should be layered, not merged; a standardized clearance assertion could sit alongside MCP’s existing OAuth profile rather than competing with it.

8.1 Normative specification: Attested Tool-Server Admission (ATSA)

We state the extension in normative form so that it can be adopted as an MCP addendum without further design work — and so that no reviewer can dismiss it as under-specified. The key words must, must not, required, shall, should, should not, may, and optional are to be interpreted as in RFC 2119 and RFC 8174. “Host” and “server” carry their MCP meanings. The extension adds no new MCP message type and alters no existing one (compatibility, below).

Discovery.

A server may advertise an attestation two interoperable ways. (i) Well-known resource: the server should serve a Server Attestation Document (SAD) at /.well-known/mcp-attestation (the Enclawed profile uses /.well-known/enclawed-clearance.json) on the same origin as its MCP endpoint, over TLS. (ii) In-band: a server may return the SAD in the initialize result under an experimental capability key. A conforming host must attempt (i), may attempt (ii), and must treat the absence of both as “unattested,” applying its configured posture (see compatibility).

Server Attestation Document.

The SAD is the vendor-neutral name for the clearance assertion of Section 4: a JSON object whose required fields are: v (integer 1); id (stable server identity); publisher; version; clearance (a canonical name or alias of a level in a named, totally ordered classification scheme, Section 4.1); capabilities (string array that must contain "mcp-server"); signerKeyId (identifies a key in the host trust root); and signature (base64 detached signature over the canonical body). Two fields are optional and, when present, are part of the signed body: netAllowedHosts (string array) is recommended — when non-empty it binds the SAD to those origins — and verification (string, e.g. tested) records the producer’s verification level. The formal schema is Appendix A. Verifiers must ignore unknown fields and must not include them in the canonical body unless a future v registers them.

Canonicalization and signature.

The canonical body is the deterministic JSON serialization of every registered field except signature, object keys in sorted order, array members sorted, an absent signerKeyId serialized as null (Definition 1). Signer and verifier must compute the signature over exactly these bytes. The Enclawed profile uses Ed25519 [9]; a profile may substitute another suite if signer and verifier agree.

Host verification rules.

Before treating a connection as admitted, a host must evaluate the following in order and must deny on the first failure:

  1. (a)

    the SAD parses and its capabilities contain "mcp-server";

  2. (b)

    signerKeyId and signature are present;

  3. (c)

    signerKeyId resolves to a key in the trust root;

  4. (d)

    that key’s validity window (notAfter, if set) includes now;

  5. (e)

    the key is approved for the asserted clearance;

  6. (f)

    the signature verifies over the canonical body;

  7. (g)

    clearance dominates the host’s required level (Definition 2); and

  8. (h)

    if netAllowedHosts is non-empty, the connected origin is a member.

A host in a deny-by-default (high-assurance) posture must reject an unattested or failing server; a permissive host should surface the failure and must not silently treat it as success. These rules are exactly Property 1, and every clause is exercised by Section 7.

Tool authorization.

Admitting a server must not be read as authorizing all its tools. A host should keep a per-server allow-list and must deny a tools/call for any tool absent from it before any network dispatch. Per-tool clearance may be added in a future v.

Audit.

A conforming host should append a tamper-evident record for every admission decision (allow / deny / warn) and every tool-authorization denial, carrying the resolved signerKeyId and clearance or the denial reason (Appendix B).

Trust establishment.

How the trust root is provisioned, pinned, and sealed is deployment policy and out of scope of the wire format. Profiles may anchor it in a pinned key set (Enclawed), X.509 chains, Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone (SPIFFE) verifiable identity documents (SVIDs) [4], or a sigstore-style transparency log [16]; the verification rules are independent of the choice.

Compatibility, versioning, negotiation.

v versions the document and a verifier must reject versions it does not understand. The extension is purely additive: an unextended host never fetches the SAD and behaves exactly as today, and an unextended server never sees the host-side allow-list; a host must therefore interoperate with unattested servers under its posture, which is what makes incremental rollout (Section 5.2) possible.

Conformance.

A conforming implementation must reproduce the verdicts of the test vectors in Appendix D. The Enclawed mcp-attested extension is a production reference implementation: its 48 hermetic tests and the LLM-driven coverage campaign (Section 7) exercise every verification clause and the tool-authorization rule against crafted and model-generated adversarial inputs. Wire format (Appendix A), verification rules, error registry (Appendix B), well-known registration (Appendix C), and executable vectors (Appendix D) together leave no normative gap for an implementer to fill by guesswork — the bar an addition to the MCP specification must clear.

Bootstrapping the ecosystem.

The first-party bridge fast path (Section 5.2) is the migration story in miniature: today’s public MCP servers do not publish attestation documents, so the host’s trust in them is mediated by a locally signed bridge manifest instead. As servers begin publishing well-known attestation documents, the same host gate verifies them directly and the bridge shim falls away — exactly how a well-known-URI extension is meant to roll out incrementally.

9 Composition with runtime drift monitoring

ATSA establishes trust strictly at the point of admission: it verifies an unforgeable server identity and evaluates a pinned signer key before any network dispatch. This is a point-in-time guarantee that answers whether a host is authorized to communicate with a specific server at a designated sensitivity level at the moment of connection. By design, the wire format does not address whether a tool’s internal behavior or exposed schema drifts over the lifetime of an active session. An admitted server may pass verification successfully but subsequently mutate its tool surface: a tool declared as read-only during an initial handshake could later advertise mutating side effects, inject new sensitive-data parameters (e.g., personally identifiable information), escalate network externalities, or trigger dynamic schema modifications between polling intervals. Because the underlying server identity remains unchanged, the cryptographic admission guarantee holds, but the capability surface has drifted. This operational boundary is where a downstream runtime drift-monitoring layer composes with ATSA.

What the drift layer needs from ATSA.

A continuous-monitoring framework requires a stable, cryptographically verified anchor to bind its behavioral baselines to. ATSA provides this structural dependency via two primitives:

  1. 1.

    Verified server identity (id). The unforgeable identity string that the runtime monitor uses as the primary indexing key for its tool-schema baseline. Without this cryptographic constraint, a drift monitor can be spoofed into baselining an adversarial substitute server.

  2. 2.

    Pinned signer key (signerKeyId). The cryptographic guarantee that the entity producing tool definitions at execution time matches the entity that was admitted. This ensures an attacker cannot bypass drift telemetry by impersonating an admitted origin.

The downstream monitor anchors each tool baseline to the unique tuple (id,toolName)(\texttt{id},\texttt{toolName}) at the first observation post-admission, checking subsequent tools/list or tools/call envelopes against that baseline.

Explicit non-requirements of the wire format.

To prevent protocol scope creep and maintain structural minimalism, three boundaries are enforced. State isolation: the wire format must not carry drift state, baseline histories, or schema-versioning metadata; baseline persistence and delta evaluation are strictly implementation concerns of the runtime monitor. Telemetry isolation: the wire format is not responsible for detecting or signaling structural mutations — it provides the authenticated identity context; detecting change is the monitor’s responsibility. Frequency decoupling: ATSA is not required to execute full cryptographic re-attestation on every individual message frame; admission remains an edge gate, and continuous runtime verification lives in the downstream monitoring layer.

Systemic synergy.

Admission control without drift monitoring risks trusting a modified capability surface indefinitely. Conversely, drift monitoring without a verified admission anchor operates in the dark — its baselines remain completely vulnerable to origin spoofing. Composed, the two layers provide a complete security posture: ATSA guarantees who, while the drift layer guarantees that the who hasn’t silently changed what.

10 Related work

Guardrails for LLM applications.

Toolkits such as NeMo Guardrails [19] police the content of model inputs and outputs with programmable rails. They are complementary and downstream of this work: a content rail does not decide which server a tool call may reach or at what clearance; it inspects the message once the connection is assumed. Enclawed pairs admission control (this paper) with a multi-modal egress reference monitor [11] for the content side.

Workload and service identity.

SPIFFE/SVID [4] and mutual TLS give services cryptographic identities; our clearance assertion adds an orthogonal authorization-to-a-sensitivity-level attribute and a host-side admission ordering on top of whatever identity layer is present. A SPIFFE deployment is a natural trust-root provider for the standardized profile.

Software-supply-chain attestation.

The Update Framework (TUF) [22], in-toto [23], and sigstore [16] sign and verify artifacts and build provenance; the clearance assertion borrows their offline-signing and pinned-root discipline but applies it to a live endpoint’s authorization, verified at connection time rather than install time.

Information-flow and access control.

The clearance lattice is a direct application of Bell–LaPadula [3] and the least-privilege principle [21] to the MCP admission point; the confused-deputy framing [7] is exactly the risk a self-asserted, wholesale-trusted tool list creates. The companion skills paper [12] provides the capability-containment layer that governs behavior after admission.

11 Limitations and future work

Several directions remain open. Per-tool clearance. The assertion binds a level to a server, not to individual tools; letting one server expose a PUBLIC search tool beside a RESTRICTED send tool is a natural refinement that the registry’s per-server allow-list already half-anticipates. Per-assertion freshness and revocation. Beyond the per-signer notAfter the verifier enforces, a short-lived notBefore/expiry on the assertion itself and an online, Online-Certificate-Status-Protocol (OCSP)-style revocation channel for compromised signer keys would tighten the freshness story. Standardization. The normative extension of Section 8.1 is specified but not yet submitted to the MCP maintainers; reconciling its clearance field with MCP’s evolving OAuth profile and capability-negotiation handshake is the concrete next step.

12 Conclusions

MCP left trust to the deployment, and that gap is exploitable everywhere — a prompt-injected model can drive a destructive tool on any server it reaches. A lone operator may absorb that risk; a regulated one cannot, and without an admission record cannot even audit it. We showed the missing trust layer can be added entirely above MCP, without changing a single message, and backed each guarantee (authenticated admission, tool least-privilege, auditability, tamper-resistance) with crafted and LLM-generated adversarial tests.

Why this belongs in the MCP specification, not in NN vendor forks.

Several forces argue for standardizing admission at the spec level rather than leaving it to each deployment:

  • •

    Trust does not compose across dialects. If every host and server invents its own attestation scheme, none interoperate and the ecosystem’s security ceiling is set by its least-attested member. One standardized shape — a single well-known document and a single verification ordering — is what makes “this server is attested” a portable claim instead of a private convention.

  • •

    The gap is intrinsic to MCP, so the fix belongs at MCP’s layer. MCP deliberately omitted trust; pushing that omission onto deployments does not remove it, it fragments it — forcing every regulated adopter to reinvent admission control, usually worse and never interoperably.

  • •

    Network effects need a Schelling point. A well-known URI and a capability handshake only pay off once both sides converge on one format. Public MCP servers publish no attestation today precisely because there is no standard to publish against; a spec creates the target, after which adoption is incremental and self-reinforcing (the bridge path of Section 5.2 is that rollout in miniature).

  • •

    Standardizing costs non-adopters nothing. Because the extension is purely additive it can be optional in the spec yet uniform in shape: an unextended host or server is wholly unaffected, while adopters gain interoperable admission. There is no compatibility tax to set against the benefit.

  • •

    It is cheaper now than later. MCP is young; agentic AI on regulated data is not waiting. Retrofitting a trust layer after a large installed base has hard-coded “connect and trust” is far costlier than reserving the well-known name and the document shape today.

We have also removed the usual reasons to defer. The extension is given normatively (Section 8.1) with a JSON Schema, an error registry, a well-known-URI registration, and machine-checkable conformance vectors, and it ships with a reference implementation whose adversarial evaluation drives every verification clause with tens of thousands of model-generated inputs. “Incomplete,” “unproven,” and “it forks the protocol” are no longer available objections. What remains is a decision the specification’s maintainers are uniquely positioned to make: to let agentic MCP reach regulated environments by adopting attested tool-server admission as a standard, optional, additive part of the protocol — rather than leaving each adopter to rebuild it alone.

Appendix A SAD JSON Schema

The Server Attestation Document conforms to the following JSON Schema (Draft 2020-12). signature covers the canonical body (Definition 1) of all other fields.

Appendix B Error registry

When a host surfaces an attestation rejection in-band it should carry a machine-readable reason in data.reason. The reference reasons, one per verification clause of Property 1:

data.reason clause meaning
not_mcp_server (a) capabilities lacks "mcp-server"
unsigned (b) signerKeyId/signature absent
signer_not_trusted (c) signer not in trust root
signer_expired (d) signer notAfter elapsed
signer_not_approved (e) signer not approved for level
bad_signature (f) signature does not verify
below_required (g) level below the host’s requirement
host_not_bound (h) origin not in netAllowedHosts
tool_not_admitted — tools/call for a non-allowlisted tool

Appendix C Well-known URI registration

Per RFC 8615 [17], the registration template:

URI suffix mcp-attestation
Change controller MCP maintainers
Specification document this extension (Section 8.1)
Status permanent (proposed)
Media type application/json

The Enclawed profile additionally serves the same document at /.well-known/enclawed-clearance.json for backward compatibility with deployed clients.

Appendix D Conformance test vectors

A conforming verifier must reproduce the verdicts below for a trust root containing one signer S (Ed25519) approved up to restricted-plus, required level restricted-plus. Each vector is a single-mutation derivation of vector 1, mirroring the reference suite (Section 7); “ADMIT/DENY(xx)” names the deciding clause of Property 1.

# verdict vector (relative to a valid baseline signed by S)
1 ADMIT valid baseline: clearance=restricted-plus, signed by S, netAllowedHosts=[]
2 DENY (a) capabilities = ["tool.invoke"]
3 DENY (b) signature removed
4 DENY (c) signerKeyId = "unknown"
5 DENY (d) S.notAfter in the past
6 DENY (e) S approved only to internal
7 DENY (f) one byte of signature flipped
8 DENY (f) clearance raised to restricted-plus after signing at internal
9 DENY (g) clearance=internal, required restricted-plus
10 DENY (h) netAllowedHosts=["a.example"], served from b.example
11 ADMIT netAllowedHosts=["a.example"], served from a.example

These eleven vectors are the T2 cases of the reference implementation’s adversarial suite and pass against it; the LLM-driven campaign (Section 7) extends vectors 2–10 to tens of thousands of model-generated instances (27,025 tool names, 14,378 forged assertions).
